Hartgen Archaeology’s report identified the site
as once belonging to a man named John Dennick. A
trip to the Albany Co. Hall of Records was in order.
Their staff has always been quite helpful any time
I’ve called or made a trip down. Looking at the
grantor/grantee records revealed that John Dennick
purchased 2 parcels of land totaling 65 acres from
the Cregier family back in 1863, thus was the reason
the Dennick name was not seen on earlier maps of
that area. The Cregier indenture mentioned the
name of Jacob Seamon or “Seaman” as once being
affiliated with the property. I’m not a genealogist
and while conducting some basic research on the
Seamon name, I’ve found variations including the
more common spelling of Seaman, but the typed and
written versions of the last name clearly appear to be
“Seamon.”
An 1810 Census of the Town of Stillwater, Sara-
toga Co. showed that a Jacob Seamon resided there.
In the land lease index of the VanRensselaer Manor
Papers indicated that a Jacob Seamon signed an
early lease of land in the East Manor of Rensselaer-
wyck in 1773, prior to the American Revolution, so
if any of you Genealogists out there have the time to
nail down the name of Jacob Seamon, I’ll be happy
to email you what little information I have, but the
topic of this newsletter relates to John Dennick and
family. My thought regarding Jacob Seamon is that
he was the original tenant on the Van Rensselaer
land along Dennison Road later in the 18th Century
after moving from the East Manor (Rensselaer Co.)
and possibly the builder of the cellar hole and struc-
ture it supported. The land was then obtained by
Cregier who may have rented out the little home-
stead to Dennick for a period of time before Den-
nick actually purchased it in 1863.
The Dennick name appears in the records of both
the Niskayuna and Lishakill Reformed Churches.
The Lishakill Church was an offshoot of the earlier
Niskayuna Reformed Church, the two having sepa-
rated in 1853. The area of Denison road is between
these two churches. The death records of the
Lishakill Church revealed that John Dennick

The book “Blind Peter” was published in Albany,
N.Y. in 1876, so it appears that John Dennick had
been struck blind sometime before 1876. The 1871-
72 Town of Watervliet Tax Ledgers (recently dis-
covered in the attic of the old Ostrom home, now the
offices of the Evergreen Memorial Cemetery on
Central Avenue in the Lishakill area of Colonie)
could reveal about when that happened. The 1871-
72 Ledger reveals that John Dennick sold his 65
acres of land “and Buil.” (Building), to William
Dennison. By 1880 John Dennick is now residing
on the Albany and Schenectady Road, having pur-
chased 40 acres of land from the “late Col. H. Lans-
ing”. Coincidently, it is the 1880 Census that re-
veals that Cornelius Lape Sr. is now living with his
daughter Eleanor Margaret (Lape) Dennick but his
whereabouts apparently unknown (or unwanted) by
other members of the Lape family. By 1897, John
& Eleanor Dennick’s son William is shown as the
owner of the 40 acres of land on the Albany and
Schenectady Road.
It seems that Cornelius Dennick left N.Y. State
for Chicago, Ill. Where he married a woman named
Rosa Benz on Sept. 17, 1883. This connection is
confirmed through estate records on file at Albany.
His brother William Dennick eventually obtains (or
inherits) the 40 acres of land that John Dennick pur-
chased from the Lansing’s as John and his wife El-
eanor eventually moved to Albany.
